The live substantive issue remains the lift-stay motion at Dkt. 146, filed August 7. What is established: service has been completed per the BNC certificate at Dkt. 158, and the response clock under Bankr. S.D. Tex. practice before Judge Lopez is running. Under the standard 14-day timeline absent an agreed order, a response deadline of approximately August 21 would fall three days before the August 24 second-day hearing — making it a live candidate for that hearing's agenda either as a contested matter or by agreed resolution. The two affidavits at Dkts. 156 and 157, also August 7, are most likely evidentiary support for Dkt. 146 or the emergency motion at Dkt. 145, but that interpretation remains unconfirmed until the documents are pulled from PACER. The volume of new appearances — at least ten counsel entries in two days — is notable as a signal that parties with discrete interests (secured creditors, suppliers, or potential buyers holding contract rights) are positioning ahead of the second-day hearing, though no specific interest can be attributed to any appearance without pulling the underlying documents. 
The second-day hearing is scheduled for August 24, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. CT before Judge Lopez in Case No. 26-90737.

The August 7 docket is procedurally dense but substantively mixed: twelve entries across Dkts. 146–157, dominated by attorney appearances and two affidavits, with one entry of real structural consequence — Dkt. 146, a motion for relief from the automatic stay. A lift-stay motion at this stage of the case is the first signal that a creditor or counterparty has concluded it cannot wait for plan confirmation to assert rights against specific collateral or property, and it will force the debtors and the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (constituted August 6, Dkt. 137) to defend the scope of the § 362 stay on an expedited timeline. The subject matter, movant identity, and collateral at issue are not specified in the docket entry, and the motion's content has not been confirmed from a primary-source pull; those facts are material and should be verified directly from the docket before any creditor response is calibrated. What can be said with confidence: under Bankr. S.D. Tex. local practice before Judge Lopez, a lift-stay motion typically triggers a 14-day objection window absent an agreed order, meaning a response deadline could fall before the August 24 second-day hearing — the next hard date on the calendar.

The two affidavits at Dkts. 156 and 157, also filed August 7, are unspecified in the ground truth as to filer and subject matter. In context — filed the same day as the lift-stay motion and five pro hac vice admissions — the most plausible read is that they are evidentiary submissions in support of either the lift-stay motion or the emergency motion filed August 6 at Dkt. 145 (whose subject remains unconfirmed). Neither interpretation should be treated as established until the documents are pulled. The continued volume of pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 149–153, five in a single day, following Dkts. 139 and 141 on August 6) reinforces what the appearance notices at Dkts. 147, 148, and 154 confirm: the adversarial bench is now fully assembled, with multiple out-of-district counsel carrying substantive mandates. Each new admission corresponds to a party that has committed resources to active participation, not passive monitoring — consistent with a case where 
holders of more than US$400 million in general unsecured claims
 have significant recovery exposure at stake — __[The Spirits Business](https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2026/07/rndc-begins-bankruptcy-process/)__.

Taken together, the August 7 filings do not move the case's structural posture — the committee is formed, the emergency motion is pending, and the second-day hearing remains the controlling event — but the lift-stay motion introduces a discrete litigation track that runs in parallel to the August 24 agenda. Creditors and rights-holders should treat Dkt. 146 as a priority pull: the movant's identity and the asset or claim at issue will determine whether the motion is an isolated creditor action or a bellwether for a broader challenge to the stay's perimeter. The schedules of assets and liabilities and statements of financial affairs remain due September 23, 2026 (the 59-day extension deadline), and the committee's investigation into prepetition asset transfers — including the more than US$700 million in tax distributions to direct equityholders reported in court filings — __[New Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Filing – Republic National Distributing Company LLC](https://www.petition11.com/p/rndc-chapter-11-bankruptcy-filing)__ — will not have its first comprehensive documentary foundation until those schedules land. The next concrete milestone is August 24, 2026 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, Judge Lopez, 1:00 p.m. CT): the second-day hearing at which interim orders are expected to convert to final, the committee makes its first public appearance, and any unresolved emergency or lift-stay matter will be on the docket.

items.body_md:
The most consequential entry since yesterday's briefing is Dkt. 145, filed August 6: an Emergency Motion whose subject matter is not specified in the ground truth but whose procedural posture demands attention. Emergency motions in large Chapter 11 cases are typically filed under Bankruptcy Local Rule 9013 when a matter cannot wait for the next scheduled hearing — here, the second-day hearing set for August 24 in Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, before Judge Lopez. The nature of the relief sought is not yet confirmed from the docket entry alone, and the committee formed the same day under Dkt. 137 will have standing to weigh in; its counsel should be pulling that filing immediately. Whatever the subject, the motion's emergency designation means Judge Lopez will likely set an expedited briefing and hearing schedule that compresses the August 24 timeline or creates an intervening hearing date — a development creditors should track for objection deadlines that may ripen before the second-day hearing.

Alongside the emergency motion, Dkt. 144 carries a Statement filed August 6, the nature of which is also unspecified in the ground truth. In context — filed the same day the U.S. Trustee published the committee appointment notice and one day after PBGC filed dual appearances — the statement is most plausibly a party-in-interest disclosure or position statement staking out a creditor's or the U.S. Trustee's posture on a contested matter. It warrants a direct pull to confirm the filer and substance. The continued accumulation of pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 139 and 141) reinforces the picture of a case where the adversarial bench is now fully assembling: each new admission corresponds to an out-of-district attorney joining a party with a substantive, not merely monitoring, role. 
RNDC carries roughly US$400 million in obligations to unsecured creditors, many of whom are smaller suppliers that face material financial difficulty of their own if recoveries fall short
 — the depth of creditor engagement the docket reflects is proportionate to that exposure.

On the transactional side, the nunc pro tunc motion at Dkt. 123 — the debtors' request for retroactive authority over RNDC New York, LLC's sale and related restrictive covenants — remains unresolved and is almost certain to be folded into the August 24 second-day agenda. The newly constituted Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (Dkt. 137) now has estate funding and full 11 U.S.C. § 1102 standing to investigate that transaction, and its first concrete leverage point remains conditioning non-objection on disclosure of the full economics of the New York disposition. 
Court filings indicate the debtors made more than US$700 million in tax distributions to direct equityholders
 — __[New Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Filing – Republic National Distributing Company LLC](https://www.petition11.com/p/rndc-chapter-11-bankruptcy-filing)__ — a figure the committee's professionals will weigh against the prepetition asset sale proceeds as they map the scope of any avoidance or clawback analysis. The schedules of assets and liabilities and statements of financial affairs remain due September 23, 2026, the 59-day extension deadline; those filings will be the first comprehensive on-record accounting of estate assets and intercompany flows, and they will anchor both the committee's investigation and the adequacy analysis of the joint disclosure statement filed at Dkt. 118. The next hard deadline is August 24 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, Judge Lopez, 1:00 p.m. CT): the second-day hearing at which the committee will make its first public appearance, interim orders are expected to convert to final, and the emergency motion at Dkt. 145 — if not resolved on an expedited basis before that date — will be on the table.
